item.title: A Bootiful Podcast: Can Java be more performant than Rust? Andrew Lombardi has the numbers
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! What happens when a longtime Kotlin and JVM fan - my friend Andrew Lombardi - decides to take on the latest “rewrite everything in Rust” hype with AI in the driver’s seat? In this episode, Josh sits down with community legend Andrew Lombardi for a fast, funny, and deeply technical conversation about his wild experiment: porting a real application to Kotlin to see how it stacks up against the much-hyped Rust rewrite.

Andrew breaks down what sparked the project, why the original benchmark caused such a stir, and how AI made what would once have been an unthinkable rewrite suddenly feel like a practical weekend challenge. Along the way, he digs into token costs, benchmarking pitfalls, caching surprises, framework parity, JVM performance, memory tradeoffs, and why Kotlin’s readability and type system make it a compelling choice for large systems.

If you care about performance, architecture, AI-assisted development, or just want to hear two seasoned developers gleefully dissect a spicy tech controversy, this one is absolutely worth a listen.

item.title: This Week in Spring - October 13th, 2026
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! Welcome to another rip-roarin' installment of This Week in Spring! This one I am writing from beautiful Carmel-by-the-Sea in sunny California's Bay Area, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. As I sit here, I'm enjoying a cup of coffee and bemusedly enjoying the amazing content in this week's roundup. We've got a ton of stuff to dive into, so let's do it!

  • Have you seen the new features in Jobrunr 9? You can easily see which step failed, find the job behind a slowdown, stop a job run without losing work, and start jobs within milliseconds. It's awesome! (And it's on the Spring Initializr, too)!
  • The GeeksforGeeks.org blog has a post about structuring a Spring Boot application and its packages. Unfortunately, it describes the traditional layered approach to architecture, and this is exactly how I would not layer my application. Instead, prefer Spring Modulith's approach, which allows you to rotate your layers 90 degrees and group things by feature, not by architectural layer.
  • I don't know if I agree with everything in this roadmap on learning Spring, but I do like that somebody's tried to document it.
  • An interesting watch by SivaLabs on scaffolding applications with Progen CLI
  • Speaking of Siva, I was happy to sit with him and do a joint video looking at some of the new features in IntelliJ IDEA at the recent IntelliJ IDEA conf. A ton of fun, as always, and I hope you get something out of it
  • At the same show, my friend and Spring AI lead Christian Tsolov looked at agentic patterns and tool calling with Spring AI - super interesting watch!
  • I was thrilled to sit with legendary Java luminary Kohsuke Kawaguchi (creator of Jenkins!) and catch up in last week's installment of A Bootiful Podcast!

item.title: A Bootiful Podcast: legendary Java developer Kohsuke Kawaguchi
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! In this episode, we catch up with one of the most influential engineers in modern Java history - Kohsuke Kawaguchi - for a wide-ranging conversation that’s equal parts tech retrospective, career reflection, and future-gazing.

It all starts with a chance reunion at a Java documentary screening in the Bay Area, where familiar faces from Sun and Oracle, old friends, and long-time admirers gathered to celebrate the ecosystem that shaped a generation. From there, the conversation opens up into a fascinating tour through the history of Java, XML, and the tools that quietly powered the industry.

Our guest looks back on his work at Sun, where he helped build XML and web services infrastructure in the JDK, and on the hobby projects that became beloved utilities for developers everywhere. We hear the origin stories behind Com4J, his XML schema validator, and his daemonization tool, along with the ideas that made them so useful in the first place: making Java more practical on the desktop, in Windows environments, and in the messy real world of software integration.

Of course, no conversation with him would be complete without talking about Jenkins. He shares the story of how a personal frustration with broken builds led to Hudson, then Jenkins, and eventually to one of the most important CI platforms ever created. We dig into why it took off, what problem it solved, and how its plugin-based architecture reflected a broader philosophy of openness and modularity.

Then the conversation turns to the present and future. He explains Launchable, the company he started to make test execution and CI workflows dramatically more efficient, and how that work eventually found its way back into CloudBees. From there, we shift gears entirely into his current chapter: time away from full-time leadership, long-distance cycling adventures across France and Italy, cooking, travel, and the kind of creative freedom that comes from stepping back.

And yes, we go deep on AI. What does someone who has spent decades building developer infrastructure think about coding agents, open models, and the future of software? His take is thoughtful, practical, and unmistakably informed by years of shipping real tools: AI is changing software development fast, but the winning systems may be the ones that integrate intelligence into existing workflows rather than forcing everyone into one giant chat interface.

If you care about Java history, CI/CD, open source culture, developer tools, or just hearing a brilliant engineer think out loud about where technology is headed next, this is an episode you won’t want to miss.

item.title: This Week in Spring - October 6th, 2026
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! It's another exciting week in the wonderful community, and this week I'm writing from awesome Antwerp, Belgium, site of the legendary Devoxx Belgium show. I've been coming here for most years since 2010, and the show is simultaneously new and exciting every year, while also structurally familiar and wonderful. It's awesome to be back. This time around, I'll be talking about Spring Security and Spring Boot 4.x. We've got a lot to get into this week so let's do!

  • Spring AI lead Christian Tsolov has a wonderful post on using Spring AI to build modular RAG solutions with TypeSafe Jev
  • this is an interesting open-source project to give you visibility into your code's "knowledge graph," called OneLens
  • that is, of course, a natural successor to his post from 21 September looking at TypeSafe Jev and Spring AI
  • it was a lot of fun being on Spring Office Hours to chat about the future of software
  • in last week's A Bootiful Podcast, I was thrilled to be joined by my friend Andres Almiray to chat about JReleaser
  • a nice, quick video called Top 5 Spring Boot Best Practices Every Developer Should Know
  • this is an interesting Java Spring Boot backend series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gJrjgg1KVL4) from a year ago that has more than 1.1 million views! :D
  • this is a nice video introducing how to master Spring AI
  • and here's another complete Java and Spring Boot course with Spring AI, RAG, and AI agents
